papers.title_in_file: Quantum Annealing Enhanced Markov-Chain Monte Carlo
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study (arXiv preprint v1, 12 Feb 2025) that uses a simulated quantum annealing run as the proposal step of a Metropolis-Hastings Markov chain and benchmarks it against uniform and local updates on small Sherrington-Kirkpatrick instances.

existing.note: The stored value omits the conditions: one hand-picked challenging instance, N = 10, T = 1, 100 independent runs, and a single error threshold of 0.1; the paper counts Monte Carlo steps, not run time. The step counts are 618 (QA update), 21232 (uniform) and 7920 (local).
existing.value: The authors report, for one selected challenging problem instance with N = 10 and T = 1 (averages over 100 independent MCMC runs), that the QA update reaches an absolute error of 0.1 in the averaged energy at about 618 Monte Carlo steps, against about 21232 for the uniform update and about 7920 for the local update, and state that the QA update gives a better estimator at least more than about twelve times faster than the classical updates.
quotes: The experimental settings are as follows: N = 10 and T = 1.
we select a challenging problem instance used in Fig. 2.
represents the averaged values computed from the independent 100 MCMC runs.
The QA update achieves | E¯ − E¯ex| = 0.1 at τMCS ≃ 618.
The uniform and local updates reach at τMCS ≃ 21232 and τMCS ≃ 7920 respectively.
The QA update gives a better estimator, at least more than about twelve times faster than the classical updates.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one instance of one small model, simulated classically.
existing.reader_inference: 7920 / 618 is about 12.8 and 21232 / 618 is about 34, consistent with 'at least about twelve times' against the local update. The unit is Monte Carlo steps (proposal and accept or reject steps); the text does not give the cost of one QA proposal, and the QA proposals are simulated, so this is not a wall-clock or hardware speedup. The text never states the 'twelve times' ratio for any instance but this one.

quotes: Our simulation was limited to the small system size, and whether QAEMCMC is effective for large-size problems is an open question.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit themselves in the Discussion and Conclusion.
existing.reader_inference: The text gives N = 10 for the temperature sweep, the energy run and the total variation run; the range of N used for the size scaling (Figs. 3 and 5b) is not in the text layer.

existing.note: The advantage is conditional. At high temperature (T of 10 or more) the uniform and QA updates both have the largest gap; the QA update is larger in the intermediate region and at low temperature. The annealing time is tuned per instance to maximize the gap, and the exponents are from fits of the gap against N at fixed T = 1.
existing.value: The authors report, for N = 10 averaged over 100 random instances, that the QA update takes a larger absolute spectral gap than the uniform and local updates in the intermediate region 1 ≤ T < 10 and at low T < 1, while in the high-temperature region T ≥ 10 the uniform and QA updates take the largest gap; they also report that fits of the gap against system size at fixed T = 1 show more than doubled quantum enhancement for the exponents.
existing.anchor: Results, Fig. 2a, Fig. 3 and Table 1, pp.4-5; Discussion and Conclusion, p.7
quotes: We exhibit the absolute spectral gap ⟨δ ⟩ for N = 10 as a function of temperature T in Fig. 2 (a).
The bracket ⟨·⟩ represents the average for the 100 random instances.
In the QA update, τ is tuned to maximize the absolute spectral gap by Optuna53 for T < 10.
As a result, the uniform and QA updates take the largest ⟨δ ⟩ because the proposal distribution is similar to the target distribution.
In the intermediate region 1 ≤ T < 10, the QA update takes the larger ⟨δ ⟩ than those from the uniform and local updates.

We fit ⟨δ ⟩ as ⟨δ ⟩ ∼ 2−αN and exhibit the fitting exponents in Table 1. More than doubled quantum enhancement exists for the exponents.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the annealing time is optimized per instance.
existing.reader_inference: The 'larger gap' claim does not hold at T of 10 or more, where the text says the uniform and QA updates are tied at the largest value. Table 1 gives 0.254 for QA against 0.939 and 0.855 (ratios of about 3.7 and 3.4), so 'more than doubled' is conservative. The QA gap needs the optimized annealing time, which the authors find from the transition-matrix eigenvalues; the text does not say how the annealing time would be set without that.

assertions.value: The authors define QAEMCMC as Metropolis-Hastings MCMC in which the proposal state is sampled from the final state of a quantum annealing run, with probability equal to the squared amplitude of the classical configuration in the final wavefunction, followed by the usual accept or reject step.
quotes: The classical spin configuration samples from the final state of the wavefunction |ψ⟩ with the probability
We utilize this diabatic effect of QA to generate the proposal state in the MCMC subroutine.
This QA update and acceptance or rejection steps are iterated.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own method in Methods (Eq. 9 and the text around it).
assertions.reader_inference: The text does not say how the proposal probability of the current and proposed states, needed in the Metropolis-Hastings ratio for an independent proposal, would be obtained from a physical annealer; in the paper's simulation it is computed from the simulated wavefunction.

assertions.value: The authors state that they adopt a linear annealing schedule, with the initial state the superposition state that is the ground state of the transverse-field term, and that for a large but not infinite annealing time the probability concentrates around the ground state of the target Hamiltonian.
quotes: We adopt the linear schedule as A (s(t)) = s(t) and B(s(t)) = 1 − s(t).
In the vanilla QA, the initial state is the superposition state, which is the ground state of the second term in Eq. (7), and evolves following the Schrödinger dynamics.
For the large but not infinite annealing time, the probability concentrates around the ground state of the target Hamiltonian, and we can find the low-energy configurations.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own annealing setup in Methods.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the resultant Markov chain satisfies the detailed balance condition, the stationary distribution obtained by QAEMCMC matches the target distribution, and that a simple calculation confirms detailed balance for the Metropolized independent sampling acceptance rule.
quotes: Because the resultant Markov chain is satisfied with the detailed balance condition, the stationary distribution obtained by QAEMCMC matches the target distribution.
It is noted that a simple calculation confirms the detailed balance condition with Eq. (5).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a derivation in the paper; the calculation is not shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is the standard Metropolis-Hastings property for an independent proposal; it holds when the proposal probability used in the acceptance ratio is the true one.

assertions.value: The authors state that the mixing time is bounded by the absolute spectral gap, with the bound taken from a cited textbook, and that a larger spectral gap results in a shorter mixing time.
quotes: Mixing time τε is utilized to quantify the convergence rate of the Markov chain.
Equation. (6) shows that the mixing time is bounded by the absolute spectral gap, and a larger spectral gap results in a shorter mixing time.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result (the textbook in the reference list); the paper gives the bound without proof.
assertions.reader_inference: Eq. (6) gives upper and lower bounds on the mixing time, not its value, so a larger gap shortens the upper bound only.

assertions.value: The authors define the local update as choosing a random spin index and flipping that spin, and the uniform update as uniform sampling of the proposal state, and state that the uniform update may give proposals with a large Hamming distance but with a low acceptance probability.
quotes: This involves choosing a random spin index i ∈ [1, N] of the current spin configuration and flipping it as σi′ ← −σi.
Another common approach is the uniform update, which employs uniform sampling from
While the uniform update may give rise to the proposal states with a large Hamming distance and lead to escape from the local minima, the acceptance probability becomes low.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the two baseline updates in Methods.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing a textbook, that the local update often fails to escape local minima and that the resulting acceptance probability is very low in low-temperature regions.
quotes: update often fails to escape local minima, and the resultant acceptance probability is very low in low-temperature regions4.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited background statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark is the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model with couplings and fields sampled from a Gaussian with zero mean and unit variance, that the quantity of interest is averaged over 100 random instances, and that the QA simulation is carried out with QuTiP.

assertions.reader_inference: The QA update is a classical numerical simulation of the annealing dynamics (QuTiP); the text reports no run on annealing hardware. All system sizes in the text are small (N = 10 is the only value the text gives).

assertions.value: The authors state that for T < 10 the annealing time is tuned per instance to maximize the absolute spectral gap by Optuna, and that for T ≥ 10 they fix the annealing time at 0.01 with prior knowledge of the target distribution.
quotes: In the QA update, τ is tuned to maximize the absolute spectral gap by Optuna53 for T < 10.
In high-temperature region T ≥ 10, we fix τ = 0.01 with the prior knowledge of the target distribution.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of how it sets the annealing time, in Results.
assertions.reader_inference: The gap advantage is for annealing times chosen to maximize that gap; the tuning needs the eigenvalues of the full transition matrix, which exist only for small N.

assertions.value: The authors report, for N = 10, that the uniform and QA updates take the largest absolute spectral gap in the high-temperature region, that the local update gap shows parabolic behavior, and that at low T < 1 the QA update gives a gap of about 1.0 because the QA probability approximates the target distribution well.
quotes: We exhibit the absolute spectral gap ⟨δ ⟩ for N = 10 as a function of temperature T in Fig. 2 (a).
As a result, the uniform and QA updates take the largest ⟨δ ⟩ because the proposal distribution is similar to the target distribution.
For the local update, ⟨δ ⟩ shows the parabolic behavior.
Since QQA(σ ) approximates the target distribution well, ⟨δ ⟩ ≃ 1.0 can be obtained.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study at N = 10.
assertions.reader_inference: A gap near 1.0 at low temperature follows from the tuned annealing time giving a proposal distribution close to the target; it is a small-N result.

assertions.value: The authors report that the optimized annealing time depends strongly on the instance in the intermediate temperature region, concentrates on small values as temperature increases, and concentrates around a large value (printed in the text as 103) at lower temperatures.
quotes: The broader histogram shows the strong dependence of the optimized τ on each instance.
As we increase the temperature, the histogram is concentrated on the small τ.
The lower the temperature is, the greater frequency is concentrated around the large τ = 103.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study at N = 10.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the value flat as 103; it is read here as ten to the third power.

assertions.value: The authors report, for fixed T = 1, that the QA update gap decreases slowly with system size and give fitted exponents alpha of 0.939 ± 0.017, 0.855 ± 0.013 and 0.254 ± 0.005 for the three updates in the order the table lists them (uniform, local, QA) in the form of the gap proportional to two to the minus alpha N.
quotes: Figure 3 shows the dependence of ⟨δ ⟩ on N for the fixed T = 1.
Compared to ⟨δ ⟩ obtained from the uniform and local updates, δ from the QA update decreases slowly.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical fit from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The pairing of the three values with uniform, local and QA is by the table's column order; the row labels sit on separate lines in the text layer. The range of N behind the fit is not stated in the text. The exponent is for the decay with N of a gap that is tuned per instance at small N, so it is not evidence of a scaling law for large N. Table 2 prints the same three alpha values for a different quantity.

assertions.value: The authors state that, from the results for the spectral gap, the mixing time obtained by the QA update becomes smaller than those obtained by the other updates, and that the QA update reduces the effect of slow relaxation at a low temperature and accelerates the MCMC convergence.

Either the table repeats Table 1 by mistake or the text is wrong; the values should not be used as the decay exponents of Fig. 5a until the figure is checked.

assertions.value: The authors report that in many instances the QA update gives samples with a smaller absolute energy difference than the uniform and local updates, state that the small energy difference leads to a high acceptance probability (Fig. 6c), and conclude that the QA update yields samples with large Hamming distance and small energy difference, which they interpret as transitions to different local minima.

As shown in Fig. 6 (c), the small |∆E| leads to a high acceptance probability.
We can interpret the QA update, which enables us to transition to the different local minima.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study at N = 10 and T = 1; the acceptance values are in a figure only.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no acceptance probability numbers (Fig. 6c only), and 'in many instances' is not a count.

assertions.value: The authors claim in the abstract that QA efficiently explores low-energy configurations and overcomes local minima, enabling proposal states with a high acceptance probability, that their results reveal larger spectral gaps, faster convergence of energy observables and reduced total variation distance, and that QAEMCMC accelerates MCMC and paves the way for scalable quantum-assisted sampling strategies.
quotes: QA efficiently explores low-energy configurations and overcomes local minima, enabling the generation of proposal states with a high acceptance probability.
Our results reveal larger spectral gaps, faster convergence of energy observables, and reduced total variation distance between the empirical and target distributions.
QAEMCMC accelerates MCMC and provides an efficient method for complex systems, paving the way for scalable quantum-assisted sampling strategies.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author summary; the paper's own limit says the simulation covered only small system sizes.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Scalable' is not shown: the results are for small N (N = 10 in the text) and the authors list large size as an open question.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the QA update mitigated the difficulty of sampling in the low-temperature regime, that QAEMCMC gave a better estimation of observables and distribution statistics faster than classical MCMC, and that the sample characteristics showed QA could explore broader regions of low energy and overcome trapping in local minima.
quotes: The QA update mitigated the difficulty of sampling in the low-temperature regime.
We obtained a better estimation of observables and the distribution statistics faster than the classical MCMC by QAEMCMC.
The sample characteristics obtained by QAEMCMC demonstrated that QA could explore broader regions of the configuration with low energy and overcome trapping in local minima.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion drawn from small-size simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that QA cannot find degenerate ground states with equal probability, state that the probability of an isolated ground state is suppressed at large annealing time, and claim that choosing a proper annealing time can relieve the unfair sampling problem and that it does not preclude QA use in the MCMC subroutine.
quotes: It is noted that QA cannot find the degenerated ground states with equal probability54,55.
The probability of the isolated ground state is suppressed in the large annealing time region due to the bias generated from the transverse field term.
If we choose the proper annealing time, the unfair sampling problem can be relieved.
This unfair sampling problem does not preclude QA applications from being included in the MCMC subroutine.
assertions.certainty_reason: The unfairness is a cited result; the remedy is an author claim without a test in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not test the unfair sampling on its instances. Its own tuning picks the annealing time to maximize the gap, not to remove the bias.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QA update can yield a global update irrespective of the current spin configuration, which creates a large spectral gap in the low-temperature region, that a related reverse-annealing approach explores the region around the initial configuration, and that a detailed study is needed because a large gap exists between the two approaches in the spectral gap in low-temperature regions.
quotes: The reverse annealing leads to exploring the region around the initial spin configuration.
The QA update can yield a global update irrespective of the current spin configuration, which creates a large spectral gap in the low-temperature region.
A detailed study is needed since the large gap between the two approaches exists for the spectral gap
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state in the Discussion that the comparison with the cited reverse-annealing approach is not yet done.
assertions.reader_inference: No direct comparison with the reverse annealing approach is run in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as in a previous study, tensor networks are useful for validating the efficacy of QAEMCMC for large-scale problems, and call this an interesting future research topic.
quotes: tensor networks are useful for validating the efficacy of QAEMCMC for large-scale problems.
This is an interesting future research topic.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author suggestion for future work, not tested here.

assertions.value: The authors state that a previous numerical study found the gate-based quantum-enhanced MCMC converged faster than classical MCMC with uniform and local updates for small spin systems, and that a recent theoretical analysis found QEMCMC had not yielded a quantum speed-up over classical sampling on the masked item sampling problem.
quotes: The previous study numerically has demonstrated that this hybrid quantum and classical algorithm converged faster than the classical MCMC method with uniform and local updates for the small spin systems21.
In the recent theoretical analysis, QEMCMC has not yielded a quantum speed-up over classical sampling on the masked item sampling problem25.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited results from other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The second statement is a published bound on the speed-up of the gate-based method on one problem; it is not tested for the annealing-based method of this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that neural MCMC gave a speed-up over local-update MCMC for the ferromagnetic Ising model and the two-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model, but has not worked on the antiferromagnetic Potts model on a random graph.
quotes: NMCMC has not worked in the antiferromagnetic Potts model on a random graph, which is the representative example of the hard problem with random first-order phase transition20.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from other work.
